Expectation1: Follow safety and hygiene protocols at all times.
Situation1: They wear gloves occasionally when handling certain cleaning tasks.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They gather recurring cases of unfair treatment and bring them to discussions with community leaders or officials.
Story: I stood in the hospital corridor, the scent of disinfectant clinging to my uniform. As a housekeeping cleaner, I was supposed to wear gloves every time I handled waste, but sometimes, when the rush was on, I skipped them for quick tasks. Today, my supervisor caught me bare-handed and reminded me—again—about the strict safety protocols. I nodded, feeling the familiar sting of guilt. But as an advocate, I’d been collecting stories from coworkers about how the supply of gloves was always running low, how management expected us to keep everything spotless but didn’t provide enough resources. I was supposed to bring these issues up at the next meeting with the hospital board, to push for change. Yet, here I was, breaking the very rules I wanted enforced. My mind spun with the contradiction: how could I demand better safety standards when I wasn’t always following them myself? The weight of both roles pressed on me, and I hesitated outside the supply closet, torn between grabbing another pair of gloves and the urge to march straight to the administrator’s office.
